{{Short description|Manifold modeled on Banach spaces}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''Banach manifold''' is a [[manifold]] modeled on [[Banach spaces]]. Thus it is a [[topological space]] in which each point has a [[Neighbourhood (mathematics)|neighbourhood]] [[homeomorphic]] to an [[open set]] in a Banach space (a more involved and formal definition is given below). Banach manifolds are one possibility of extending manifolds to [[Infinity|infinite]] [[dimension]]s.

A further generalisation is to [[Fréchet manifold]]s, replacing Banach spaces by [[Fréchet space]]s. On the other hand, a [[Hilbert manifold]] is a special case of a Banach manifold in which the manifold is locally modeled on [[Hilbert space]]s.

==Definition==

Let <math>X</math> be a [[Set (mathematics)|set]]. An '''[[Atlas (topology)|atlas]] of class''' <math>C^r,</math> <math>r \geq 0,</math> on <math>X</math> is a collection of pairs (called '''[[Atlas (topology)#Charts|charts]]''') <math>\left(U_i, \varphi_i\right),</math> <math>i \in I,</math> such that

# each <math>U_i</math> is a [[subset]] of <math>X</math> and the [[Union (set theory)|union]] of the <math>U_i</math> is the whole of <math>X</math>;
# each <math>\varphi_i</math> is a [[bijection]] from <math>U_i</math> onto an [[open subset]] <math>\varphi_i\left(U_i\right)</math> of some Banach space <math>E_i,</math> and for any indices <math>i \text{ and } j,</math> <math>\varphi_i\left(U_i \cap U_j\right)</math> is open in <math>E_i;</math>
# the crossover map <math display=block>\varphi_j \circ \varphi_i^{-1} : \varphi_i\left(U_i \cap U_j\right) \to \varphi_j\left(U_i \cap U_j\right)</math> is an [[Smooth function|<math>r</math>-times continuously differentiable]] function for every <math>i, j \in I;</math> that is, the <math>r</math>th [[Fréchet derivative]] <math display=block>\mathrm{d}^r\left(\varphi_j \circ \varphi_i^{-1}\right) : \varphi_i\left(U_i \cap U_j\right) \to \mathrm{Lin}\left(E_i^r; E_j\right)</math> exists and is a [[continuous function]] with respect to the <math>E_i</math>-[[Norm (mathematics)|norm]] [[topology]] on subsets of <math>E_i</math> and the [[operator norm]] topology on <math>\operatorname{Lin}\left(E_i^r; E_j\right).</math>

One can then show that there is a unique [[topology]] on <math>X</math> such that each <math>U_i</math> is open and each <math>\varphi_i</math> is a [[homeomorphism]]. Very often, this topological space is assumed to be a [[Hausdorff space]], but this is not necessary from the point of view of the formal definition.

If all the Banach spaces <math>E_i</math> are equal to the same space <math>E,</math> the atlas is called an <math>E</math>'''-atlas'''. However, it is not ''[[Wiktionary:A priori|a priori]]'' necessary that the Banach spaces <math>E_i</math> be the same space, or even [[isomorphic]] as [[topological vector space]]s. However, if two charts <math>\left(U_i, \varphi_i\right)</math> and <math>\left(U_j, \varphi_j\right)</math> are such that <math>U_i</math> and <math>U_j</math> have a non-empty [[Intersection (set theory)|intersection]], a quick examination of the [[Derivative (generalizations)|derivative]] of the crossover map
<math display=block>\varphi_j \circ \varphi_i^{-1} : \varphi_i\left(U_i \cap U_j\right) \to \varphi_j\left(U_i \cap U_j\right)</math>
shows that <math>E_i</math> and <math>E_j</math> must indeed be isomorphic as topological vector spaces. Furthermore, the set of points <math>x \in X</math> for which there is a chart <math>\left(U_i, \varphi_i\right)</math> with <math>x</math> in <math>U_i</math> and <math>E_i</math> isomorphic to a given Banach space <math>E</math> is both open and [[Closed subset|closed]]. Hence, one can without loss of generality assume that, on each [[Connected space|connected component]] of <math>X,</math> the atlas is an <math>E</math>-atlas for some fixed <math>E.</math>

A new chart <math>(U, \varphi)</math> is called '''compatible''' with a given atlas <math>\left\{\left(U_i, \varphi_i\right) : i \in I\right\}</math> if the crossover map
<math display=block>\varphi_i \circ \varphi^{-1} : \varphi\left(U \cap U_i\right) \to \varphi_i\left(U \cap U_i\right)</math>
is an <math>r</math>-times continuously differentiable function for every <math>i \in I.</math> Two atlases are called compatible if every chart in one is compatible with the other atlas. Compatibility defines an [[equivalence relation]] on the class of all possible atlases on <math>X.</math>

A <math>C^r</math>'''-manifold''' structure on <math>X</math> is then defined to be a choice of equivalence class of atlases on <math>X</math> of class <math>C^r.</math> If all the Banach spaces <math>E_i</math> are isomorphic as topological vector spaces (which is guaranteed to be the case if <math>X</math> is [[Connected space|connected]]), then an equivalent atlas can be found for which they are all equal to some Banach space <math>E.</math> <math>X</math> is then called an <math>E</math>'''-manifold''', or one says that <math>X</math> is '''modeled''' on <math>E.</math>

==Examples==

Every Banach space can be canonically identified as a Banach manifold. If <math>(X, \|\,\cdot\,\|)</math> is a Banach space, then <math>X</math> is a Banach manifold with an atlas containing a single, globally defined chart (the [[identity function|identity map]]). 

Similarly, if <math>U</math> is an open subset of some Banach space then <math>U</math> is a Banach manifold.  (See the [[classification theorem]] below.)

==Classification up to homeomorphism==

It is by no means true that a finite-dimensional manifold of dimension <math>n</math> is {{em|globally}} homeomorphic to <math>\Reals^n,</math> or even an open subset of <math>\Reals^n.</math> However, in an infinite-dimensional setting, it is possible to classify "[[well-behaved]]" Banach manifolds up to homeomorphism quite nicely. A 1969 theorem of [[David W. Henderson|David Henderson]]{{sfn|Henderson|1969|p=}} states that every infinite-dimensional, [[Separable space|separable]], [[Metric space|metric]] Banach manifold <math>X</math> can be [[Embedding|embedded]] as an open subset of the infinite-dimensional, separable Hilbert space, <math>H</math> (up to linear isomorphism, there is only one such space, usually identified with <math>\ell^2</math>). In fact, Henderson's result is stronger: the same conclusion holds for any metric manifold modeled on a separable infinite-dimensional [[Fréchet space]].

The embedding homeomorphism can be used as a global chart for <math>X.</math> Thus, in the infinite-dimensional, separable, metric case, the "only" Banach manifolds are the open subsets of Hilbert space.
